utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Two little points of housekeeping, just before we call the witness. Mr. Milovancevic, I just wanted to check out with the Defence the estimate of the time for the next witnesses, and also to know who is the next witness coming so that if it is the one that I think it is, I can raise the next point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. The next witness is Mr. Barriot. In our estimation, he will be a live witness and there is a change, Your Honours. There should have been two witnesses covering the same topic, and we thought it would be more efficient to bring only one witness, to call only one, to save time and simplify the proceedings. We also felt that live testimony would help us be more expeditious. Mr. Perovic will conduct the examination-in-chief and, in our estimation, we will need up to two sessions for the examination-in-chief, not more. That, of course, is only an estimate, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Examination-in-chief only, two sessions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, thank you for giving that estimation and for telling us who is next. Indeed, I did suspect that it was going to be Mr. Barriot who was coming next, and I wanted just to say, moving now to the next point, that based on the summary that you filed, it looks like there are parts of his summary that deal with areas that have been excluded in the oral order that we made the other day. If you look, for instance, at -- yeah, there are a number of places that I picked up that I think relate to areas. There is one, two, three, four, five, the sixth paragraph, for instance, on page 2; the third paragraph from the bottom on page 2; the second paragraph on -- from the bottom on page 2; the second paragraph from the top on page 2; and I'm not quite sure of the relevance of one, two, three, four, the fifth paragraph from the top on page 2; and the last paragraph on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we are referring to the summary by which we announced this witness on the list of witnesses, we bore in mind the instruction issued to us by the Trial Chamber and we shall seek not to repeat those themes at all and have the witness testify only about issues which have not been mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm looking at the summary which I think was filed very recently, apparently it's called the updated -- it's not titled that way but when it came I was advised that it was the updated summary. It stands alone on a piece of paper. It's not part of the bunch that you gave, but anyway, I've raised those issues and we will look out for them as the witness carries on with his evidence. You may call the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall bear that in mind, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry, Mr. Milovancevic, what has changed now that the original estimate was plus/minus two hours?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that was the estimate on the assumption that there would exist a written statement that would be admitted into the file. Right, 92. So we have abandoned that in order to simplify the procedure and gain time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated, sir. I'm sorry about that. Yes, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Barriot. As one of the counsel on the Defence team of the accused, Milan Martic, I shall be conducting the examination-in-chief today. I should like to ask you to pause between my questions and your answers in order to enable the interpreters to do their work, and I should like to also ask you another thing. My questions will be concise and I should like your answers to be just as concise, and I thank you in advance for that. Mr. Barriot, for the record, would you give us your first name and last name.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: My name is Patrick Barriot. I was born on the 5th of October, 1955, in Bedarieux, in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What are you by nationality and a citizen of which state are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I am a French citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What is your profession?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I am a medical doctor. I'm specialised in anaesthesiology, emergency medicine, disaster medicine, and emergency toxicology, and I served in the French army for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: So you have a degree in medicine?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I have a degree in medicine. I am a specialist also. I served in the army during 25 years. I left with the rank of colonel, and I'm currently a specialist serving in hospitals, working in hospitals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: During your military service, were you awarded any honours; and if so, what particular honours are in question?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I received a number of distinctions. I am chevalier of the Order of the Merit. I received four medal for acts of bravery. I received them from the prefect of the French police in Paris. And I received three letters, first from the Ministry of Defence, from the Chief of Staff of the army, and from the Ministry of Cooperation; letters of congratulation for having served France; and given generous image of the French country during operations abroad, operations conducted to help the civilian population in these countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: What profession are you pursuing today, what particular occupation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I am currently a specialist working in hospitals, and I am also a lecturer in many schools of medicine, universities in France. I am also a member of a group that works and studies anti-terrorism operations, working on the risks caused by nuclear, biological, and chemical weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barriot, for these particulars from your curriculum. Were you assigned at any moment during your career to any duties in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I was deployed in the former Yugoslavia, more precisely in Croatia, in Krajina, and that was in the year 1994. At the time I held the rank of lieutenant-colonel, and I was appointed and assigned as a blue helmet at the 1st Infantry Battalion of the -- of UNPROFOR, the 1st Battalion was a French battalion and it was stationed in Glina. The medical unit I was a member of was deployed in Topusko next to Glina, in the south sector of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Had you been to Yugoslavia before that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. It was the first time I went to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: And before you arrived in Yugoslavia, did you know anything about the situation in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: When I arrived in the former Yugoslavia with Eve Crepin, the only thing I knew about the former Yugoslavia was what I had read in the newspapers or heard in the news, on television, so I had no personal opinion. I only had the information that were broadcasted by the French media.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, what was UNPROFOR's task in the protected zones? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Theoretically, the mission of UNPROFOR in these protected or safe areas that were introduced in 1992, the mission was to be there between the Serbs and the Croats, to interpose themselves in order to protect the Serb population in the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Barriot, what were your specific duties, yours personally, within the UNPROFOR mission?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I was an anaesthesiologist at the surgical unit based in Topusko, as I said earlier on, but since there was little work to do, little care to be provided to the French soldiers there, I was a member of a medical team that would go to all the villages in the surrounding area. We would go to isolated farms in order to provide medical care to people who needed it, and since the hospital in Glina had no anaesthesiologist anymore, Dr. Knezevic was the held doctor of the hospital, asked me if I would be able to work there as an anaesthesiologist, in the operation theatre every morning. Therefore, every day I would work as an anaesthesiologist at the Glina hospital. That was the medical part of my work. Apart from this, as superior officer, I would take part in all the briefings organised by UNPROFOR, and these meetings would take place once a week or twice a week, let's say, more often than not twice a week. And these -- in these meetings there would be French officers but also foreign officers, most of them being Canadians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, in the territorial sense, what area was covered by your activity, if you can tell us that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I moved around regularly on the entire -- in the entire south sector, the region of Banija, Kordun, Lika, the north of Dalmatia, and the Knin-Krajina region, and that's for the Krajina region. I would also regularly go to Bosnia, to the Bihac pocket, and I would in particular go to Velika Kladusa, where I met Mr. Fikret Abdic among others. I would also regularly go to Zagreb for missions of liaison, to liaison with my superior officers there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were there in that area, did only Serbs live in that area or were there members of other nations and ethnicities there as well?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: There were members of other ethnic groups, of course. I can state that because at the Glina hospital, you had staff members who were Croats, but a lot of Muslim patients would come to the hospital, especially wounded people from the Bihac pocket, they would come to the hospital to receive medical care there. And these patients have always been welcomed and they always received medical care at the Glina hospital. Furthermore, in 1994, during the summer of 1994, I was there when the 5th Corps of the Bosnian army under the command of Atif Dudakovic, General Atif Dudakovic expelled the partisans of Fikret Abdic from the pocket and expelled them to the Krajina region. Therefore, there were about 40.000 Muslims, supporters of Fikret Abdic, went to the Krajina to several camps, the camp of Batnoga among others, and these 40.000 Muslims received food, medical care, despite of the very difficult situation that prevailed in Krajina at the moment, and they also received medical care at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: In this connection I should like to ask you this: You have referred to this already but what was the status of primarily the Croats in the areas in which you were? Were you able to find out anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. There were two types of cases or situations. In the first-- the first case was the case of the Croats who accepted or who decided to stay in the Krajina and to live in peace with the Serbs. I met these Croats in isolated areas, small villages, isolated farms, and these people were never attacked, were never threatened by the Serbs. They lived in -- they lived peacefully, but there were other Croats who had decided to leave the Krajina region and to go to other cities, such as Zagreb. And mostly because the living conditions in the Krajina were extremely difficult, the economic situation was extremely bad because of the embargo imposed on the region, and therefore life was easier outside of the Krajina; but I never noticed any threats, any forced expulsions. I never saw anything of the kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barriot. I will now show you on the screen document 1D0-048, which is one of the weekly reports of the European Monitoring Mission, and for the week which ends on the 23rd of December, 1993. Do you see that document on your screen? Can we turn to page 2 of this document, please? I'm going to read out for you the paragraph under number 4(B), which is, and I quote: "The UNCIVPOL Glina stated that of the 818 Croat families living in the Glina area, 90 per cent are living in good conditions and are accorded the same rights as Serbs. Generally, we have found that minorities are being well-treated in most of the CCAOR," which is an abbreviation which I presume refers to the Knin Krajina. You said that you arrived in the Krajina in March 1994. Did you find, when you arrived, a situation which corresponds to this description in the document of the European Union's Monitoring Mission which I have just read out to you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Absolutely. I can fully confirm this report, if I saw it correctly. This report was established at the end of 1993, and I can say that in 1994 the Croats were treated -- benefited from the same treatment in 1994 as is stated in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this document be admitted as a Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Perovic. What is this document? It doesn't seem to have a heading. Mine starts with a B, unconfirmed; then C, protests. Is that it in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the second page of this document, and the document is a weekly report of the European Union's -- European Community's Monitoring Mission for the week which ends on December 23rd, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we look at page 1, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we see page 1 of this document, please, on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: According to what I have on the screen, this document has two pages; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first page of this document, the front page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And the document has an amount of two pages; is that correct, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely so, Your Honours, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 1006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: You have already said something about this, Mr. Barriot, but I will ask you any way. During your sojourn in the Krajina, did you personally observe any pressure on the Croats or other non-Serbs to move out of the area?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. And I can say it with a great deal of certainty because I was taking part in the daily life of the citizens in the Krajina. I would go to the hospital in Glina every day to work there as an anaesthesiologist. I would move around the whole territory of Krajina. I would go to cities such as Knin, Glina, et cetera, but I would also go to the smallest villages and the -- and isolated farms. And I can state with all responsibility that I was never a witness to any acts of violence or any acts of pressure aimed at making Croats or Muslims move out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, you mentioned that a certain number of Croats left the Krajina for economic reasons. My question in this regard is the following: What was the situation you found in the Krajina on your arrival with regard to the economy?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: In 1994, the situation, as far as the economy was concerned, was disastrous. It's something that you were able to notice every day in -- because the Krajina citizens were missing the most basic things, such as soap, washing powder. It was extremely difficult to find candles because the -- at most times there was no electricity. There was a primary school next to the surgical unit in Topusko, and the students there, the pupils there, didn't have any thing to write with, any pens. And at the hospital, there were no antibiotics. There was -- there were not enough products to -- for the anaesthesiology department. There was something missing also at the radiology department, same for the biology laboratory. And at every level of daily life it was obvious that the citizens of the Krajina were missing the most basic commodities in their daily life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Perovic, didn't you ask about the Croats especially, having left for economic reasons, as you said? It wasn't quite clear to me actually to what sentence you referred actually when you said: "If I understood you correctly, many Croats left for economic reasons." Can you clarify that without leading that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was one of my previous questions. Your Honours, that was one of my previous questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. I understand, but to what previous answer had you referred to, to make it clear? I don't understand it. I was asking myself that already when you asked that question, but can you now maybe help us? Because I tried to find it and I didn't find it, that Croats left for economic reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness, responding to one of my previous questions, said there were two categories of the Croatian population, one part remained in the Krajina, living in the villages, while some Croats moved to cities, such as Zagreb, for economic reasons because, as the witness said, the situation in the Krajina was very difficult. That was in response to one of the previous questions, whereas my last question --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If I can assist, Your Honours I think that answer is found at page 8 -- actually starting at page 7, line 25, and continuing on to page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You may proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. My last question was what economic situation the witness found on his arrival in the Krajina, and he spoke about it; and he explained how this was reflected on the work of the hospital in Glina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Under such conditions, Mr. Barriot, were the patients in the hospital in Glina Serbs only, or were there also members of other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: There were members of other ethnic groups, as I already pointed out. There were Croats, some of them were patients, and there were a lot of Muslims. I emphasise there was absolutely no difference being made to the way people were treated, depending on their ethnic background or their religion. I remember one thing precisely. I remember a Muslim woman who had been operated on, had a Caesarean surgery and a lot of haemorrhaging, and a little blood supply that was left in the hospital was used for her for a transfusion, so it was given to her. This is to show you that there was no discrimination whatsoever in the way patients were treated, whatever their ethnic background or religion may have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, in the course of the time you spent in the area, did you have occasion to meet the local population; and if you did, how did they feel and think at the time? Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Of course. As to the contacts I had with the local population, I can say they happened gradually of course, because initially I was a foreign military. Of course I came to help them at the hospital, but it took time to, as it were, tame them, but as time went by, I got to be accepted by the population. I was invited to their homes. I attended at weddings, funerals. I can say that I really lived within the population, among them. And one thing struck me particularly, that is the fear that prevailed. These people were really terrorised. They continuously referred to World War II, to the massacres by the Ustashas. So it was all the more intense in the Glina area. You have to know that there were atrocious massacres committed by the Ustashas in the Glina church, all such memories were surface; also because the Croats, starting in 1991, would display a lot of Ustasha emblems, the red and white chequer-board.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it correct that you said you arrived there in March 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do you testify to events of 1991 then? How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I just stated, Mr. President, I did live with people who told me that every day, and also every week I attended UNPROFOR meetings, together with officers who were in charge of analysing the situation, its development, and they had been doing that since 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What you said was: "Also because the Croats, starting in 1991, would display a lot of Ustasha" -- you're not telling us something that you are told, you're telling something that -- you're putting it as if it's first-hand information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I told you, these were people I lived with in Glina, and they told me so. They saw it with their own eyes. I'm just reporting what I heard from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then say they told me. Don't say: "Also because the Croats, starting in 1991, would display a lot of Ustasha emblems, the red and white chequer-board." I'm referring specifically to what you said before I stopped you. You understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do. I do understand. I was about -- I was just developing my thoughts, you see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, develop them and then say them; don't say things first before you develop them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Perovic, in fact, Judge Nosworthy was just also pointing out to me that that's in fact an area that we had cut out in our oral decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it was not my intention to elicit such an extensive answer when I put my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, what was the attitude of the local population toward the blue helmets, to put it that way? You said something about their attitude toward you personally, as a member of the blue helmets. I'm now asking you what the attitude of the local population was towards the blue helmets in general.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, the attitude of the local population in Krajina towards the blue helmets was one of hope and confidence and trust. As I explained to you earlier, they were really terrorised. They feared an invasion of Krajina, and they set all their hopes on the international community, therefore on the blue helmets, hoping that they would therefore be protected from a renewed aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did you, in the course of your mission as a member of UNPROFOR, have occasion to go to Croatia outside the UN protected areas, to Zagreb, for example? And if you did, what was the attitude there towards members of UNPROFOR? What was the attitude of the Croatian authorities and the attitude of the population towards UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: To give you an accurate answer, I can say I would regularly go to Zagreb for liaison assignments, either to meet with our hierarchy or because we were a kind of postman, go between, between Croat citizens living in Krajina and their families in Zagreb, so we would carry their mail and parcels. We would regularly go to Zagreb. And I can tell you that the general attitude of Croats in Zagreb towards the UNPROFOR was totally different; it was characterised by manifest aggressiveness towards anybody in an UNPROFOR uniform. When we would go to Zagreb, our superior officers told us to go without uniforms, to be in civilian clothes when we were in Zagreb, for a simple reason. In the eyes of the Croats, the UNPROFOR soldiers were there to prevent the Croats from taking back Krajina by force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I believe that the first part of the question was the attitude of the Croatian authorities, and the second part was having to do with attitude of the population towards UNPROFOR; and the witness has not really effectively addressed the first part of your question. So maybe you could put it to him again and let him place the evidence before us, if he's able to.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, I asked you what the attitude of the Croatian authorities was towards members of UNPROFOR. At the same time I put another question, namely: What was the attitude of the Croatian population towards UNPROFOR? Could you distinguish between the two? Could you say something about the attitude of the Croatian authorities and then something about the attitude of the local population?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I may not have been clear enough, but I believe that there is a link there, these two aspects are intertwined. If the population was aggressive towards the UNPROFOR, they did so because they were sort of fed by the statements and the attitude of the political authorities. It was obvious that everything at the level of the Croatian political authority was done to terrorise the Serbs. I told you there were the emblems, you could see again the Ustasha emblems, especially the chequer-board; also street names, square names were changed. The square of the victims of fascism became the square of the great Croats. All the work by Mile Budak, who is an Ustasha historian, were again in vogue and they were taught in schools. The dinar was replaced by the kuna. And in the army, Ustasha ranks --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barriot. You spoke about weekly briefings with UNPROFOR officers, which you attended. I would like to know whether you had occasion to talk to UNPROFOR officers outside these meetings; and if so, what you discussed and what they told you, outside the official meetings.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand the meaning of your question, but first of all I'd like to say that it is quite normal -- when a new unit or a new surgical mobile unit would arrive, it's normal for the ones before them, the authorities would present the situation in a detailed manner and would remind them of the situation as it started. So that was quite normal. Secondly, it is also obvious that as a senior officer, I had a lot of discussions in the canteens, in -- personal discussions with numerous officers who had been there for -- some of them since 1992, and who were perfectly familiar with the situation. I also talked with foreign officers. One thing was clear and it was told us from the very beginning - I arrived in March 1994 - and all our predecessors told us this: The war is going to start again. It's going to resume in Krajina. We have many indicia showing that the Croats are arming themselves, are organising themselves, in order to take back Krajina. So there was no ambiguity in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, at that time, was there a prohibition on the import of weapons on to the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I'd say this is a follow-up question to the previous one, inasmuch as we were talking about this. Of course, this is the primary worry and concern of a military. It is the way weapons circulate, the way weapons are smuggled. It was clear that there was an embargo on arms in the entire area in place since 1991; but equally obviously, the Croats were arming themselves then with the help of Germany and the USA. In 1994, a private American military company, Military Professional Resources Incorporated, MPRI, came to settle in Croatia. They had a team in Zagreb at the level of the American embassy, and that team was responsible -- in charge of the arms smuggling and the arms supply to the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Mr. Barriot, the embargo on the import of weapons was not respected; and if I understood you correctly, the embargo was violated by the Croatian authorities with the assistance of certain foreign factors. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. You understood me perfectly. I would not say that the embargo was violated by chance; it was done on purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did the UN take any steps to sanction such violations of the arms embargo? Do you know something about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, nothing was done, no step was taken, in order to prevent the embargo from being violated. I would even say that the military were tasked to keep their eyes closed, you know, including the UNPROFOR members. As to the violations of the embargo, they had been told not to mention that in their reports. An example, in 1994, the military in my unit had seized assault weapons of American make, the MN-16, and in the Bihac pocket they had been provided by the USA to the 5th Bosnian Corps, that of Dudakovic, who had been charged with attacking the Krajina and the partisans of Fikret Abdic. So there was an obvious desire to turn a blind eye on such violation as to the arms embargo by the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Apart from this arms embargo, Mr. Barriot, to the best of your knowledge, was there any other embargo imposed by the UN on the territory of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There was a dual embargo. There was the air embargo, in trade and oil-related, on Yugoslavia; but there was also Resolution 820 of the UN Security Council prohibiting any import or export to or from the Serbian Republic of Krajina. In other words, the small republic was totally cut off, isolated, from the world; and this, as I told you earlier, resulted in total poverty for people there and it really drove a lot of them to despair.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Did this -- or was this economic embargo you have just mentioned respected, in contrast to the first one you just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. It is obvious that this embargo was totally complied with. As I told you, you could see it in the care provided to the population, who could not enjoy quality care because they lacked the bare minimum. So the economic embargo on Krajina was applied very rigorously, whilst obviously the arms embargo was continuously violated by Croatia, so it was obviously dual standards in terms of embargoes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Under these conditions, did the international community give humanitarian assistance to those areas; and if so, to what extent?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I can give you a very clear answer. There was no humanitarian assistance whatsoever given to the Serb population in Krajina. I can tell you so because I'm a specialist in humanitarian assistance. I have not seen a single NGO, be it a Medecins du Monde, Medecins Sans Frontieres. Nobody helped. I say nobody helped the Serbs in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: When did your mission within UNPROFOR end, Mr. Barriot?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: My time of service within the UNPROFOR ended in June 1994, but later on I went back to Krajina regularly, every other month, in order to work in the surgery department in the Glina hospital. With just a tiny Serbian organisation, the Krajina association founded by Mile Bucan -- and they had basically no means so I would get money out of my own pocket to buy drugs, medical supplies, which I would take regularly to the Glina hospital, which lacked everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I assume you then had occasion to meet refugees. What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Of course I did. In Krajina, I met with a lot of refugees. They had been expelled from Croatia in 1991. And they described to me the situation as it prevailed in Croatia in 1990 and 1991, at the time when they were regarded as second-class citizens, when their constitutionally established rights were abolished, when their basic rights were trodden upon. So these were people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Apart from the Serbian refugees, did you have occasion to see any other -- refugees belonging to any other ethnic groups on the territory of Krajina; and if so, which?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I met refugees from other ethnic groups, mostly Muslim refugees. There was a great number of Muslim refugees from the Bihac pocket. As I mentioned earlier on, they would come to receive medical treatment, to find refuge in the Krajina; and during the summer of 1994, these 40.000 Muslim refugees came after having been expelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting. I wanted to ask you what was the attitude of the government, the authorities, and the population in Krajina towards these Muslim and other non-Serb refugees? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I know that, because I was working in a hospital, and a hospital in a situation of that kind, the hospital is the most appropriate place to go if you want to understand the situation. When you have almost no blood supply left recognition, when you have almost no medicine, the natural reaction is to keep what little you have, to keep it for your own people, for the members of your ethnic group, but that's what -- not what happened. I'd like to repeat it. When there was a wounded Muslim, Croat patient, or -- there was no discrimination. If there were only two blood bags left, they would be given to the Muslim patient; what little antibiotics was left was given to Serbs and Muslims. There was absolutely no discrimination there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barriot. Are you familiar with the position of the Croatian authorities with regard to the resolution of the question of the UN protected zones? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I know something about that. I know what was said in the south sector for UNPROFOR, what was said by the officers of UNPROFOR, and it was that the Croats would not take that into account, the protection afforded by the United Nations, and that as soon as they would be ready to attack. That is to say, as soon as the Americans and MPRI would have provided them with the necessary logistical support and with the necessary supplies, they would attack these protected areas without any regard for their status, for their protected status.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Croatia launched any military operations vis-a-vis the UN protected zones?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I was in touch with French officers, especially people working with General Kot, who were direct witnesses of these attacks because between the years of 1992 and 1993, there were three major attacks led against these safe areas of the United Nations; the first one took part in the month of June 1992 on the Miljevac plateau, in the northern part of Dalmatia. The second --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, the Croat army, the Croatian army, attacked these safe areas deliberately and no one did anything about it; and in any case, UNPROFOR was not in a position to put an end to these operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: These operations have been discussed here and we shall not dwell on that now because of that. But from what you have seen in the field, Mr. Barriot, you are a physician but you are also a soldier of long standing, I suppose that you could answer the question: What was the weaponry that the RSK army had? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I can give you a very specific answer because in 1994, I was a senior officer of the French army, and I would go abroad on a regular basis; and therefore I was in touch with intelligence French officers from the DGSE, French Intelligence Services. And at the time the DGSE asked me to tell them about what sort of weapons systems there was in the RSK. They showed me pictures of all the types of tanks and artillery systems you can imagine; and what I can tell you is that at the time, there was no heavy-weapon system in the RSK. You had rifles, of course, a few rocket-launchers, but there was no heavy weapons system, contrary to Croatia, where you had MiG 21, heavy weapons system, weapons fit to conduct an invasion. The only type of weapons you could find in the RSK were light weapons of an exclusively defensive type.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, you said that the role of UNPROFOR had been a protective one, and you also said what the UNPROFOR officers told you. According to what you saw and experienced in the field, did the UNPROFOR mission in which you also participated, successfully perform its mission?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. My answer will be very clear about this. UNPROFOR did not perform its mission because the mission of UNPROFOR was to protect a population that was defenceless, that had no heavy weapons at its disposal. It was a defenceless population that was located in a safe area of the United Nations; and therefore, the role of UNPROFOR was to protect these civilians who were defenceless. And it was never the case, because these civilians from 1992 to 1994 were subject to attacks and to the atrocities of the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Talking about these attacks, this aggression on protected areas, UN protected zones, do you know whether any foreign states had played any role in these Croatian operations? And if that is the case, and if you do know something about it, what was that role?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: The main part was played by the United States on two levels. First of all, the American army - I'm talking about the American army, I'm not talking about NATO - the American army intervened directly to shell Serb forces in -- first of all, when they shelled the Udbina airport in 1994, and there was also of course the Knin -- the shelling of Knin, that marked the beginning of the Storm operation. Therefore, the American army intervened directly in these two cases at least. And then there was also, even more important, an indirect intervention through MPRI, Military Professional Resources Incorporated, because here you have a private military company that is under the command of the Pentagon. Its leaders or directors are former American generals, and these are the people who trained the Croatian army and armed the Croatian forces with a view to conduct the Flash operation and the Storm operation. An agreement was concluded in that respect between Gojko Susak, who was the former defence minister of Croatia, and the director of MPRI; it was called, this agreement, Assistance to Democratic Transition, that was the name of the contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, could we have a basis for what's just been said? I wonder -- just be curious to know how the witness knows that, if it's first-hand information or second-hand information, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that my learned colleague, the Prosecutor, will put his question when he examines the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, no. There has to be some basis for this to have any probative value before it can be admitted as evidence; that was the gist of my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think Mr. Perovic you need to lay a foundation. How does the witness know all this? Did he see it first-hand? Was it -- was he told by somebody?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all I can do is to ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: How did you come by this information that you have just related to us? I'm talking about this relation between this American organisation and the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: All the information I'm giving you today were given to me by senior officers of the French army and senior officers of the Canadian army who were deployed in Croatia at the time. I am a senior officer. I said that I would tell the truth here, and there is nothing more I can add. But of course, I'm not going to give you a document by MPRI; I can't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would that be a convenient point?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was just about to thank Mr. Barriot for his testimony, and that concludes my examination-in-chief. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Barriot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic. Then this is a convenient time to take the break. We'll take a short break, sir, and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Barriot. My name is Mr. Black. I'm one of the Prosecutors on this case, and now it's my turn to ask you some questions for a little while. I would say -- I'm not going to address every single topic you mentioned because the Trial Chamber knows our positions on a few things like the chequer-board symbol, et cetera. Just so you understand, it doesn't mean that we accept what you say, but I'm not going to ask you questions about that. I'm going to try to focus on other things. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Good morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I guess first of all, since we find ourselves here, do you have any views on this International Tribunal, especially about its purpose or its impartiality?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: May I give you a candid answer? I believe that this Tribunal was not set up on a legal basis, on a legal foundation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Could you explain a little bit what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I could explain a little bit. I believe that a resolution of a Security Council is not enough to establish such a Tribunal. A vote by the General Assembly of the United Nations was necessary to give the necessary legal foundation to this Tribunal; therefore, I deeply think that this Tribunal is illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about its partiality? Do you have any views about the partiality of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I have a view about it, yes. Obviously this Tribunal is a partial Tribunal. No representative of the Croatian authority was indicted; President Tudjman was not indicted. Not a single Croat minister, Muslim minister, was ever indicted; on the other hand, all the representatives of the Serb authorities were indicted. And if you look at the convictions, you see that Naser Oric was sentenced to two years in prison for the crimes he committed as if he had just stolen a motorbike, whereas all the Serbs who were convicted were convicted very strictly, received very steep convictions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That you for that. Let me ask you about a book of yours on the same subject. In fact, we could look at it on our screens. The ERN is Y0061852.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honours, there is a book that was obviously written in French. I had translated just one very small excerpt, not the whole book. I don't intend to move it into evidence. Hopefully we can deal with it using the simultaneous interpretation to read any passages that we need to other than what's been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, you see in front of us, this is your book, titled, I guess, "Our testimonies About Serbia," written by you and your partner, Eve Crepin, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. It's one of the many books we wrote together with Eve Crepin because we wrote a total of five books together about the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd ask -- this line in particular includes articles that -- some of which were separately published and some of them were authored just by you or just by her and then were collected in this work. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, that's exactly the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you to look at one in particular, and it starts at what is ERN Y00061865. If we could navigate to that on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the English translation which has been provided is -- it's actually not that clear from the English translation, but it's just a couple of paragraphs from what -- the French article that we'll be seeing. And we'll point that out so that it's clear, I hope.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The translation should be in e-court, I hope. I mean, I'm sure that it's in there. The translation may be under the specific ERN Y0061865. Okay. That's the -- and in the French we need to move ahead a couple of pages to 1865, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, you see there --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Oops, now we see the English translation. If we could have the French up on the witness's screen again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, sorry, it will just be a second. This is the first time we've used French and English documents in the trial; it's usually English and B/C/S, so we have to sort out our technical issues a little bit. Okay. I think we can proceed now. You see there--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, can you just get us to the English, please? I have French on both screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Oh, okay. Mr. Whiting says that he has English on his. I don't know if it's a question of maybe refreshing it or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I also do have English.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have the English version on paper. It would be good to have both French and English, to be sure they are accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have English now, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can we provide the interpreters with the English translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I do not have the English translation in hard copy, Your Honour. I thought since it was on the e-court system, the interpreters could access it on the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: The interpreters say they cannot access it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: They cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We do not have it in hard copy. I guess the registrar is going to save me on this one and she'll print it out and provide it. I appreciate that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, can you confirm just that you have the French version on your screen, is that right, the original version?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I do not answer what you want me to confirm -- I do not understand what you want me to confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just whether or not you see the French -- the original French version on your screen because we are having some trouble about which version is on whose screen, but you're seeing the French; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I've got pages 26 and 27 in French on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Perfect. Okay. Thank you. And what you see here is -- on the right-hand side is an open letter to -- it says: "To a friend who is or is alleged to be a war criminal"; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And this is an open letter to Milan Martic, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. It's an article we wrote together with Eve Crepin a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think, in fact, it was first published in September of 1997; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I think that's the case. We wrote a number of articles, so it's difficult for me to remember the dates of all the articles.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could focus, please, on the second paragraph in that right-hand -- the right-hand page.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I just wonder if you could -- you see the sentence that begins there with "Nietzsche, Nietzsche said." Could you read out that to the end of the page, please, for us.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Gladly, gladly. Thank you very much for the interest you have for our articles. Let me read out. "Nietzsche said that only in the sphere of the common man is the enemy always considered to be evil. The International Criminal Tribunal is the jurisdiction of the common man. War that has not lost -- that has lost none of its horror has now lost all of its honour. So-called international justice is nothing more than an adulterated ersatz of justice contrived by the victors. Its emblem should depict a greengrocer's scale, the rigged scale of a crooked grocer."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much. And that's, I take it, still your position now as you sit here, not only when you wrote this article but that's still your position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I believe that I've answered your questions very clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So far, absolutely. But this question -- I take it that this is -- the view expressed here in this article is still your position today; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Can we turn to the next page, please, in French. It's in the continuation of the same paragraph in English, Your Honour. And as I was saying, this was prepared -- of course we found out the witness was coming on Monday morning, so this was prepared -- I just got it yesterday and it's just a couple of paragraphs, which I hope is clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: There at the top left-hand corner, that -- the last sentence of that paragraph, it says that: "The Tribunal is based upon a crime against the consciousness which postulates that the army of the victors is just and the army of the vanquished is wicked." Is it still your view, sir, that this Tribunal is based upon a crime against conscience or against consciousness?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is still my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Just one more question on this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could scroll down a bit to the next paragraph there, still on the left-hand side. And this is the next paragraph in the English translation, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You see where it says: "Dear, Milan Martic. Why is your name written on these lists?" And then it says: "On Tuesday, the 2nd, and Wednesday, the 3rd, of May, 1995, on your orders, three or four Orkan rockets were launched on Zagreb killing five. The order was given in retaliation for the Croatian army's brutal invasion of Eastern Slavonia." I have a couple questions about that. First of all, you confirm here that the shelling of Zagreb was ordered by Milan Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. That's the only thing I cannot confirm. I can confirm everything else, but I do not confirm that fact. I did not have the information, the relevant information. I think I made a mistake. I do not confirm -- I would like to insist on that point, I do not confirm that it is on the order of Milan Martic that the rockets were fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, on what basis did you write that in this article in 1997 then?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I relied on false information, false data, and on the fact that I believe that President Milan Martic wanted to assume the responsibility of an act that he did not order. But since he was -- he had a very high opinion of his office as a president, he was ready to assume any kind of responsibility; but I would like to withdraw the sentence you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what's your basis for saying that Martic wanted to assume responsibility for an act that he did not order? What have you learned since 1997 that leads you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I believe you have to replace yourself in the context of the time. What was going on when these Orkan rockets were launched on Zagreb? What was going on is that the Croatian army, with the support of the United States, was shelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise for interrupting. I'm not sure you understood my question. What is it, since you wrote this article in 1997, that has now illuminated you and you realise that Martic was just trying to take responsibility for something that he didn't in fact do?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you answer, sir, can you please speak slowly. I can hear the interpreters struggling to keep pace with you. Talk slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there is already a mistake as to the date when this article was written; it was published here in this book, indeed, but it was written earlier. Therefore, these are articles that were written in the heat of the moment when these events took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let me just tell you something so that you understand it. I don't want us to get into an issue that we don't have to. You know, the Defence in this case has not disputed the fact that Mr. Martic ordered that shelling. They have other defences about why he may have done it, things like that, but just so you understand that. Do you understand what I've just told you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic. I thought it was Mr. Perovic, but anyway, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the Trial Chamber. Just a brief consultation, please. [Defence counsel confer].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Your Honours, bear with me, please. I forgot myself. I was not conducting the examination-in-chief. Everything is in good order. There is no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Yes, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Actually could we look -- I just want to address something here if we could look at the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, you had a question to the witness; it's not answered yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think my question was just if he had understood what I had said to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Do you understand what I have said about the fact that the Defence has not disputed that Mr. Martic ordered the shelling? Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But then you also wanted him to answer the question what has he learned since 1997 that changed his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I'm still on that. I want to deal with a sub-issue to help clarify this, but I haven't forgotten that question. I appreciate it. If we could look, please, at page Y0061924. It's very near the end. In fact, I think it's the second-to-last page in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Same page in the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This does not appear in the English at all, Your Honour. It's just -- this is a list of publications. I just want to establish the date of this article that we've been speaking of. Thanks, and if we could look at the right-hand side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: See the sixth entry down there, sir, there is a reference to this article that we have been discussing, the open letter, and it says that it's from September of 1997. Now, based on this list from your book, do you agree with me that the article was first written or published in September of 1997?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, no. I do not agree with you on that because these are articles that were published several times in various publications or newspapers, and I only wanted to mention the reference to Balkan info, so I do challenge the date of writing. I wrote them earlier, and this being said I want to emphasise this: You take out three words in a major article and the three words are not relevant. What was relevant was to show that this was an act of desperation in the face of the assassination of civilians by the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thanks. Please just try to focus on my questions and we'll move along more quickly. So despite the only reference in your list of publications, you insist that this article was actually written before -- much earlier than September 1997, and I think you said "in the heat of the moment when these events took place"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: More often than not, all the articles and books we wrote like this book people is assassinated and the other ones in 1995. This was written in reaction to atrocious events for the people, the Serb people, in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Now let me get back to my original question. What was it since you wrote this article, be it in 1997 or earlier than that, that has now illuminated you and made you realise that Martic was just trying to take credit for something that he did not actually do?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, as a matter of fact, I think it is the analysis of his personality which I could make as I met him. I believe he's a man who had a very high idea of his responsibility. His only objective was to protect the Serbian people in Krajina; and as any leader worthy of the name, he always covered or took on him anything done by his people below him, which is done by any good leader anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any video or heard from Mr. Martic or seen anything where he took responsibility for the shelling himself? Did you see those videos that were widely aired at the time?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I can't remember, precisely all the more so since there is a little language-related problem because Milan Martic speaks Serbian and I do not speak Serbian fluently. So there is always a bit of an obstacle because of translation problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'll try to move on to this, but I want one thing to be clear. Your sole basis for now changing your opinion and thinking that he didn't actually order the shelling is just your analysis of his personality? That's what led to you change positions?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. And sometimes there is subtle nuances that can appear in translation; it's true. But he always said, I am the president; therefore, it is my duty to take on me -- to take responsibility for things that are being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did he say that to you specifically about the shelling of Zagreb, or do you just mean on other occasions in general?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, no. I'm very specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you spoke with him about the shelling of Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Of course, of course. We spoke about the entire situation, about everything that had been done.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And he told you that he had ordered the shelling, or did he tell you something different?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. He never said that he had ordered the shelling. He only said that he was willing to take responsibility for anything that had been done by subordinates, and that he would not accept that subordinates would be jailed or convicted whilst he was the president and he was at the top of the nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How did this topic of conversation come up?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Because we talked a lot about this concept of responsibility of statehood and state. And since you put the question to me, he often repeated, I am the president. I'm here in order to ensure the safety of the Serbian citizens in the RSK, the citizens are the Serbs, and all those who want to live peacefully with the Serbs, be they Croats or Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You know, there is one other -- the next -- one of the other sentences I read, the last sentence I read out, said that -- maybe you're going to say that you can't talk about this either, but you said in your article that: "The order was given in retaliation for the Croatian army's brutal invasion of Eastern Slavonia." Do you stand by that or is that something else you want to -- you want to change now?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But this is obvious. This rocket firing is a result of the invasion of Western Slavonia, as a result of the hundreds of defenceless civilians that were massacred by the Croatian army. If you see today that two Israeli soldiers are being kidnapped, and therefore hundreds and thousands of children and women are being killed in --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I know it's tempting to make analogies to other things that are happening in the world today or at different times, but please let's just stay focused on the conflict in former Yugoslavia. I take it that in your view, the shelling of Zagreb was wholly justified by what was happening in Western Slavonia, notwithstanding the fact that there were civilian casualties in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: If the UNPROFOR had done their job properly, it would not have been justified; but inasmuch as the UNPROFOR failed to carry out their mission to protect those people, somebody had to do for them, that it was self-defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So you think under the circumstances you've described, it was justified to shell Zagreb, notwithstanding the deaths and injury to innocent civilians; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, look, now the military is going to answer you. On the one hand, it was a desperate act, it was self-defence; on the other hand, the Orkan rockets aimed at military structures, especially the Ministry of Defence. Indeed, there were casualties. But when you see that the so-called smart weapons of NATO guided by laser and GPS killed hundreds of people in collateral damage, you're not going to say that an Orkan rocket launched from Petrinja or Petrusan could have been more accurate. I'm sorry, it could not have been done; they didn't have the means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: By no means am I suggesting that an Orkan attack might have been more accurate, quite the contrary. It seems like you think you know something about this. Isn't it true that the Orkan rocket, by its very nature, if you launch it into a city, into a populated area, there are going to be civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But this is the very proof that if those Orkan rockets were fired, it shows that the RSK did not have any heavy weaponry, no heavy armaments, and all they had was these miserable poor rockets they had, and they defended themselves. This is an act of survival, an act of desperation, using whatever they had; and the only thing it goes to show is that they did not have heavy armament and no performing accurate artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. Let me show you just briefly Exhibit 91 in evidence in this case, please. Actually, Mr. Barriot, I understand that you don't speak B/C/S. Do you speak English? Do you read English?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: [In English] I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Actually I don't want to put you in a difficult position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So if we could see the last page of the English, but also I'll read it out so that it could be translated into French just so that everything is clear. Thank you. And it's those top two paragraphs in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, this is an interview with General Milan Celeketic, the commander of the SVK on the 24th of March, 1995. Mr. Celeketic there says: "In the case of the Ustasha aggression, we will certainly not miss the opportunity to hit them where it hurts the most. We know their weak spots and where it hurts the most. Weak points are city squares, and we know who goes there: Civilians. I've already said this and was criticised a little. Well, now, they may ask which squares and in which cities? I shall reply that it's a military secret. We shall make a decision about it, and I think we will be precise."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, where are you reading? I'm sorry, I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's at the very top of the last page in English, Your Honour. It's on the public screens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of the last page?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And then, Mr. Barriot, it continues it says -- Celeketic says: "It is hard to say these words because there are, as I said, civilians in the squares, innocent people. However, if we are in war and we are waging a filthy war for which they are first and foremost to blame, then there will be no mercy, not only will we be merciless but as a commander I shall decide where we will direct our attacks, when and where it hurts the most." Mr. Barriot, this doesn't say anything about military targets. It talks about intentionally targeting city squares because that's where it hurts the most.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Two observations on this text. On the one hand, this general is the one who can speak for what he said. What I do maintain is that these Orkan rockets were firing at military structures and that the casualties were collateral damage in the NATO speak, and also that this type of speech is aimed at deterring. This man thinks that he wants to avoid the invasion, the Storm and Flash operation, at all price whilst they were being prepared. It was one way of deterring the Croatian army. It was a desperate attempt to deter them. I do not think at all that this was a plan and that it was carried out in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Did you personally ever hear such comments, either from General Celeketic or from Mr. Martic that you recall?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just before -- well, actually, what's your basis -- you've insisted on the fact that military targets were the target of this attack. What's your basis for that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Because it was said so by the leaders of the RSK, but not by Mr. Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: When you say "it was said so" -- oh, so you say that you heard other leaders of the RSK say that military targets were the object of the attack? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Isn't it true that in the first day or two after the shelling, Martic took responsibility for ordering it. No one mentioned military targets at all. It was only a couple days later, once there was an international uproar over this, that this theory of military targets emerged?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: It's curious that you should say so. The international community did not feel upset by the fact that there were hundreds of children and women who were massacred in Western Slavonia, but they were in an uproar, up in arms, because there were five people killed in Zagreb. And this goes to show that there was in this terrible war really dual standards.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And it was only after that international uproar that anyone mentioned military targets in Zagreb; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: You do not place yourself back in the time. It was a period of utter confusion, that the RSK was in a state of shock, was of utter despair. They could see that the Croats were in the process of killing and butchering their families, and this was a last-ditch attempt to defend themselves. They knew that following the Storm operation, there would be the -- or the Flash operation, there would be the Storm operation; everybody knew that very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, can I interject here? I would like, sir, you to answer the question that was put to you. The question was: "Isn't it true that in the first day or two after the shelling, Martic took responsibility for ordering it?" Can you respond to that question? You were asked that question. Something else was added and then you commented upon the [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President, I cannot answer the question because I do not have the exact statements made by Mr. Milan Martic in the following days. All I can tell you is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's enough. You may carry on, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just see if I can get an answer to my last question which was: It was only after this international uproar that we talked about that this theory of military targets was talked about; correct? Or -- if you don't know, that's fine; you can say so.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, no. This idea of military targets, I knew about it from the very first shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: How? How did you know that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Because I was in touch with leaders of the RSK, especially with the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Mr. Slobodan Jarcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And when was the first time that he told you that there were military targets being targeted in Zagreb? Be as specific as you possibly can.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I will be extremely specific, because I was in charge of the office representing the RSK in Paris. In this capacity, I received the dispatches by Mr. Milan Martic to be transferred to the AFP news agency. So as of the 1st of May, I conveyed the appeals for help launched by Mr. Martic to the international community; this remained without an answer. Later on, with the first rocket shots, or fires, I knew that there were military targets being targeted. I knew it from Mr. Slobodan Jarcevic, with whom I was in direct contact, and he was the Minister of Foreign Affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Let me move on to something that you said reminded --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, before you move on, please, I'd like to ask Mr. Barriot a question. Mr. Barriot, could you please tell me, were you given specific military targets by Mr. Jarcevic, or were you just advised that generally there would be military targets? Did you have more specific information concerning which buildings might be targeted or which particularly -- which particular military objects would be targeted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a dim memory because after all this goes back over ten years, but I seem to remember that there was a Ministry of Defence and there was also a military airfield, but that's all I can tell you. This is not very precise memory I have of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And you got this information from Mr. Jarcevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And when precisely did you receive this information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't tell it to the day, but it was in the beginning of May, must have been around the 4th of May, 1995. One day or two, I can't be absolutely certain, but yes, that's about the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And did you share this information with anyone, outside of persons who were part of the Krajina authority? Did you share it with any member of the UN or any other organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I trans -- I did share this information to all organisations, to the AFP news agency, but no press release was published. But I did send some press releases for the Storm operation and they were published, but all this had been sent to the AFP news agency. All this information had been conveyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Barriot. Mr. Black, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one point of clarification, sir. You mentioned Mr. Jarcevic, but you also said "the Minister of Foreign Affairs." Mr. Jarcevic was no longer the Minister of Foreign Affairs in May 1995; correct? He no longer served in that position after April of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: That's true. For me, he remains the Minister of Foreign Affairs; that's the way I call him. But you're right. I'm not trying to sort of play on dates here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you were indeed speaking about Mr. Jarcevic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm going to change topics now for a minute. In actually around this same time in May 1995, both you and Eve Crepin became RSK citizens; isn't that right? You applied for and received RSK citizenship?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, that's not quite the way it happened. We received RSK citizenship as an honour, in an honorary fashion, for the assistance we provided to the people in need. There was no political connotation to this gesture. You know, you can be appointed honorary citizen for a city due to the efforts you deployed to help the population of that city.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
