utterances.text: But there certainly way as an official character to your appointment by Mr. Martic as RSK representative in Paris; correct? That's something that happened I guess in June or July 1995? Can you confirm that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I must have received the official letter around that date; that's true. But to all intents and purposes, I had been the representative since the -- late 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And you received -- you were appointed to that position by Mr. Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That -- how did that idea come about? Could you just very briefly say what it was that led to you being named representative of the RSK in Paris? Was it your idea or Mr. Martic's idea or how did it arise?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: It came about naturally, but I could tell you that it was a joint idea, that sort of matured as months went by, as discussions went by, because Eve Crepin and I were involved in humanitarian aid and we tried by all means to make it possible for the Krajina Serbs to have a voice in the media. So this is an idea that arose jointly as time went by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. This caused you problems, correct, at home? And in fact, it was this position as representative of the RSK which caused you to lose your position in the French army. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: It is true. There was a complaint by Mr. Mate Granic, who was then the Croatian Minister of Foreign Affairs, who complained to the UN that a French army un -- officer it would help the Serbs, and Charles Millon, the French minister, punished me for not complying with the obligation of reserve that is imposed to officers. I was not punished because I would have violated the honour of the army or because I would have collaborated with the enemy; I was punished for saying what I had seen, what I had witnessed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And in effect, you were, I guess -- correct me if I'm wrong, but you were dishonourably discharged, you lost your rank and you had to leave the army; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Your information is not accurate; it's false. My superiors offered me a kind of deal. They told me, if you decide to go back on everything you have said so far, if you say that you have been manipulated by the Serbs from the Krajina, you can remain in the army and you can continue your career, but you have to do this in writing. But if you do not accept to do that, you'll have to leave the army. Then, of course, I refused to go back on what I had said. I left the army, but I left the army with the rank I was holding, with my rights to my pension; and therefore, no sanctions were taken against me because my only fault, the only fault I had committed, was that I had told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for the explanation. I think I understand you. Do you have any regrets about sacrificing your military career to -- you know, to support the RSK, to accept this position?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. I have no regrets. Eve Crepin does not regret anything either because she also lost as much as I did; she lost her career. But we believe that the greatest injustice that can be committed is the injustice committed against an entire people, and we believed that we saved the honour the French army. And I believe that -- I must say that it's a young lady, a young woman, who saved the honour of the French army, Eve Crepin.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me move on to another topic. Just so I'm clear about this, you were in UNPROFOR in Croatia for three months, from March to June 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And you were serving as a military -- or, excuse me, as a medical officer, as a doctor basically, during that time, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I was serving as an anaesthesiologist for the forward surgical mobile unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So primarily, you were treating patients, not analysing intelligence or commanding troops in the field. Your duties were primarily medical; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. That's not quite correct. Yes, that's right, I was there as a doctor, my duties were medical; but as I said earlier on, the intelligence services, the French military intelligence services, were in touch with me and they had asked me to supply information about the weapons in circulation in the RSK. I mentioned that previously. So I would have regular meetings with the man in charge for the Yugoslavia. He would show me pictures of all types of weapons systems for me to be able to recognise them, but I didn't have to recognise anything because there were no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I'm talking just now about March to June 1994. So you're saying you were in touch with these intelligence people then, or was that something that came later?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: It took place at that time from March 1994 to the summer of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You were stationed in Glina, which is some 50 or 60 kilometres away from the headquarters in Zagreb, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, the mobile unit was in Topusko, but that's very close to Glina, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So -- and you talked about the briefings you had and that you were in contact with these intelligence officers. But you didn't have, for instance, daily access to the intelligence reports such as what those officers in the headquarters in Zagreb would have; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, but as I said earlier on, there were about two meetings a week at the battalion level, very frequent meetings, and I would go to Zagreb on a weekly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This first three-month mission in Krajina was when you met Eve Crepin; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We were working in the same hospital in Metz, before but before we didn't know each other. We actually met in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I have no intention of getting into your personal life. But just so that it's clear, since then you've been living together; correct? You're in a relationship with Ms. Crepin?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, that's indeed a personal matter. I was -- I had indeed a relationship with Mrs. Crepin to the last few days.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. I have no -- I don't want to get into that any more. I just wanted to establish that for the record. You also developed, it appears, an extremely strong bond with the Serb people in the Krajina while you were there. Is that an accurate description, an accurate statement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe that that brought us together, Eve Crepin and myself. Is that the -- it's the awareness that these people had been demonised, unjustly accused, and we decided to help these people as much as we could, considering our resources, our means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So to do that after you were no longer part of UNPROFOR, you returned several times in your private capacity; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. Eve Crepin and myself would go back very frequently, every two months or so, and we would bring supply, equipment, medical supply for the hospital, and we would stay there for two to three weeks. We would work in -- as anaesthesiologists in the surgical unit of the Glina hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. There is one thing from my notes I just wanted to get clarification from you. It's at page 13 of the transcript. You were talking about your contacts with the local population. And you said: "I can say they happened gradually of course because initially I was foreign military, of course I came to help them at the hospital, but it took time to, as it were, tame them. But as time went by, I got to be accepted by the population." I was just wondering what you meant by that, by it took time to "tame" the local population.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Sorry, either you misquoted me or I did not express myself; I said we tamed each other. In other words, I just wanted to say that we got to know each other because they would tame me as much as I would tame them, but it's a sort of affectionate way of speaking about our relationship, and it was bilateral.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks for the clarification. Another thing, at page 6, lines 1 and 2 of the transcript, you were talking -- you were asked about the task of UNPROFOR in the protected zones, the UNPAs. And you said there: "The mission was to be there between the Serbs and the Croats, to interpose themselves in order to protect the Serb population in the Krajina region." And my question is that the UNPROFOR's mission was not just to protect the Serb population, but to protect all civilians in the UNPAs; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. It was to protect all those people living in these UNPAs that were -- that had no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: One other thing, I guess while I'm on the topic of clarifications. At page 21 of the transcript, you were talking about how there was no discrimination in the hospital in Glina and you said: "The natural reaction is to keep what little you have, to keep it for your own people, for the members of your ethnic group." And then you say: "But that's not what happened." Why do you say it would be your natural reaction to keep medical supplies and life-saving techniques for members of your own ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: It seems obvious to me. If you're starving and you find a piece of bread, you're tempted to eat it yourself or to share it with the members of your family, but you're not really tempted to give it to someone else to someone who is not really close to you. What I wanted to say is that despite the dramatic circumstances, the dramatic conditions these people were living in in the Krajina, they still remained generous towards people who were not that close to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness, were you are not also speaking of the attitude of the medical personnel in this regard? And if I understood you correctly, and you included doctors of medicine, would you say it's a natural attitude of a doctor to make these differences?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not only referring to the medical staff. I was -- also to the doctors. I was also talking to [as interpreted] those working as nurses, working in the labs, and I was talking about everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Sir, please answer my question. I asked you if you included them and if you would say that about the natural attitude of a doctor of medicine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a rule in what we call disaster medicine; it's not a rule that applies in the normal circumstances. Please let me explain yourself [as interpreted]. When you're confronted with a disaster, you have to select amongst the patients. I'm a specialist in the matter. I can tell you, in some circumstances I have to make a selection; and in these circumstances, they could have made a selection but they did not do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You mean there are rules in anaesthetics and emergency medicine about selection which include criteria of certain groups of the population, social groups, or are these only medical criteria?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only medical criteria are operative, but what I was telling you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean you were telling me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was saying that the cases I referred to were desperate cases. These people could have been left to die, but nevertheless everything was done to save them. They were given medicine, treatment, although their state of health was desperate and -- but these people were non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: And you would regard this an extraordinary phenomenon just in these cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that's displaying a great deal of generosity, and I think that I'm in a position to be able to assert that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: As a doctor of medicine, you mean, so this is why I asked you that, you know. Thank you. You may proceed please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, you testified that while you were in the RSK, the RSK had no heavy weapons, they only had light weapons that were -- I think you said "exclusively defensive."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that's on -- for the benefit of counsel and the Chamber, on page 22 and 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes you said: "The only type of weapons you could find in the RSK were light weapons of an exclusively defensive type." You don't deny, though, that the RSK had its own army, the SVK, at the time, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I know it. I'm talking about operative weapons. I'm not talking about a few tanks, a few very antiquated tanks that didn't not have any fuel to run.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, obviously the SVK also had at least some sophisticated weapons, like the Orkan multiple-barrel rocket-launcher that we mentioned earlier, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I don't believe that you can call them sophisticated weapons, these Orkan rocket-launchers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The SVK also had combat aircraft in 1994, 1995, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: These planes never took off. They were not operational. In any case, the US army had destroyed all the systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me ask to you look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's R0014619, if we could see that on our screens, please, and I'm afraid this is one that I only have in English, I believe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: As you can see - I'll try to explain it if you have any trouble with the language - but this is a letter from the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for the former Yugoslavia under UNPROFOR letter-head to Mr. Martic on the 15th of November, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And if we could scroll down a bit, please -- actually to the last -- that last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The second sentence says: "A combat plane based at Udbina is also reported to have launched a missile attack against Bihac town on 9 November with civilian casualties and considerable material damage." Udbina is within the territory of the RSK; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So this refers to a combat plane taking off from RSK territory; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: This is a lie. The same lie that was propagated that at the time of the Knin attack, the aim was to justify the American attack against the Udbina airport. They stated that the radars had spotted a NATO airplane and then they opened fire, but this was just a way of justifying the attacks of the US army planes on Serb defensive systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So in your view, what Mr. Akashi says here is a lie? There is just no truth to it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I believe that he's justifying things that had been decided previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 1007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, just please permit me once again. Mr. Barriot, what makes you say with such certainty that it's a lie? Why do you declare it a lie, on what basis?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I declare it on the basis of the analysis conducted by intelligence services, who were perfectly well informed about what was going on. I'm not talking on the basis of statements made by politicians or statements of a highly political nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So you would not be relying on your own personal knowledge? You are relying on information supplied to you or not supplied to you by intelligence services?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm relying on facts. I'm relying on the fact that the US army shelled the Udbina airport, and I'm relying on the fact that its combat aircraft, American aircraft, that launched the first missiles during the Storm operation. These are facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Black, please do continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just before we leave that, sir, you say that these are facts and that makes them so. But I mean, these are just things that you were told, right? You didn't personally witness these; you're just accepting the word of someone else.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, but you do exactly the same here at the Tribunal. That was written up in all the newspapers. It's not even a secret. Journalists have said it. It's been filmed, so you can't really deny it. If you deny it, then you do not accept anything. If you take -- if you have that point of view, then nothing can ever be proven.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I assume that what you're talking about is the distinction between hearsay, and you're right second-hand information is accepted here but it's accepted as such. And there is a distinction that's made between first-hand information and second-hand information. Do you have a difficulty distinguishing yourself about what's first-hand knowledge and what's second-hand knowledge?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, no. I can make the distinction without any problem. Do you deny the fact that the US army shelled the Udbina airport? Do you deny the fact that two aircrafts from the Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier conducted shelling at the beginning of the Storm operation? Do you deny that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, first of all, it's not my position to deny these sort of things, but don't assume what I accept or deny or what I'm going to say to you. Your job here is to answer my questions, okay. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yeah, but I've answered your questions. I told you that these -- this information had been given to me by sources from French intelligence services, and at the beginning of my testimony I said that I will tell the truth. I can't add anything to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. So when you say something is a fact, you mean it's something that you could have heard from someone else and you accept as true, yourself personally? Just so we are clear about what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, it's not hearsay. It's a number of arguments, information from intelligence services, the reports made by journalists on the spot. It's a great deal of information. You're saying it's very vague, but it's not the case. It's a whole series of facts that corroborate each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me move on to another document, I think, at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Or actually -- excuse me, Your Honour, if I could just take a moment. I forgot whether I'd asked for this last document to be admitted into evidence. Yes, okay, 1007. Thank you very much. Could we see R0014455 on the screens, please. Actually -- and if we could go to the second page, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, you see here this is a letter, again to Milan Martic. This time it's from the force commander of UNPROFOR. So this is not a politician, this is a military man speaking here. It's dated the 18th of November, 1994. And if you see it, that second paragraph, it says: "At approximately 1100 hours this morning, two 'Orao' planes that had taken off minutes earlier from Udbina airport struck Bihac with one cluster bomb and one napalm bomb. We have irrefutable proof that the above-mentioned planes belong to your forces." Sir, you have no grounds to dispute what's written in this document, do you, by an UNPROFOR force commander do you, or do you contend that this also is a lie?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I'm only saying that these irrefutable proof they are talking about, they are not produced here; therefore, I suppose following your way of -- your reasoning, I believe that we should take his word for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, please don't follow my way of reasoning. I want to know what you think. I mean, you have no reason to dispute what's written in this letter; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Yes, I do, because, as you said if -- using the argument you use against me, I use this against the general who wrote this letter. I do not see in this letter any irrefutable proof that these planes were indeed coming from Udbina and were supposed to attack the place they'd attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: -- I'm not asking you whether you can see irrefutable proof in the letter, okay. Do you accept or do you not accept what's stated there, that these two planes took off from Udbina and struck Bihac? Do you accept it or don't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, I don't and I'll tell you why I don't accept it, because there was -- the American army wanted to destroy the airport at Udbina; that's why I'm very suspicious about any type of information of the kind. We can seriously doubt what is saying by UNPROFOR, because at the end of 1994 UNPROFOR did not conduct its mission of protection in the southern area of the zone and we are here precisely talking about zone south in the protection area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, there becomes Exhibit Number 1008.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think we are at the time of our regular break now as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes. Before we go, I would like to ask two questions, or rather, one question in relation to this document. May I? Mr. Barriot, would a cluster bomb be an offensive or defensive weapon? And in relation to a napalm bomb, could you also apply the question to that also, that bomb also, in terms of weaponry? You'd spoken before about defensive weapons and I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, there has never been any napalm bomb in Krajina. As for cluster bombs, the word of cluster bomb is a very vague term. We would need to know whether we are talking about bombs aimed at piercing an armour, the armour of a tank, or aimed at attacking a column of tanks that were conducting operation in the Bihac pocket, because we know that the 5th Corps was there and was getting ready to attack the Krajina region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: All right. Given that you do not believe that the RSK had, is it napalm - how is it pronounced? - bombs, could you still apply my question to the type of weaponry that it is? Would it be an offensive or defensive, to apply the descriptions which you had used much, much earlier on in your evidence? Accepting that you say that the RSK did not have this type of weaponry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you use a cluster bomb and napalm bomb, it can only be defensive weapon in front of an attack, in preparation. But I'm very surprised because as far as I know, no victim was ever recorded, no person who would have been burned by a napalm bomb. Because people who fall victim to that type of weapon, a napalm bomb, are burned in a very specific manner, and this could not have passed unnoticed in the medical centres of the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's time to take a break. We'll come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry about that. Yes, Mr. Black, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, you testified that the Krajina received no humanitarian assistance during the time that you were there. It's true, isn't it, that UNPROFOR, and in particular the UNHCR, did provide humanitarian aid to the Krajina in 1994 and in early 1995?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct. In 1994, when I was a blue helmet in Krajina, in Glina, there was an office of the UNHCR headed by Bertrand de Lapresele and there was some degree of humanitarian assistance but it was totally disproportionate with regard to the needs on the spot. At any rate, there was no NGO. The NGOs -- they only helped the Croats and the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could perhaps look at a document just quickly. It's actually one that I didn't get uploaded into e-court, Your Honours. I have hard copies. I've given a hard copy already to the Defence and one for the interpreters. So if a copy could be given to the witness and to the Bench, please. Thank you very much. For the record, this, is -- bears the ERN 01733271, and I'll get -- we'll get into this e-court just as soon as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, you see that this is a document from the UNHCR. It's a letter, actually, to Mr. Martic dated the 8th of March, 1995. And if you just look with me at the first paragraph, let me read it out so that you can also have the benefit of the oral translation. It says: "Dear Mr. Martic, I have the honour to refer to our meeting in Knin on Tuesday, 21 February. You will no doubt recall that on that occasion, I emphasised that UNHCR was finding it increasingly difficult to justify continuing to meet 100 per cent of the needs in the UNPAs while obstructions to the passage of aid convoys to the Bihac enclave through territories under your control meant that UNHCR had only be able to deliver close to 20 per cent of the needs there since May 1994." First of all, this says that they were meeting 100 per cent of the needs in the UNPAs. Do you dispute that characterisation?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, I do dispute that categorically. When you are in the Glina hospital which is the most important hospital in the area, when you do not have antibiotics, you do not have any anaesthetics, you don't have any blood supplies, you don't have any biological reaction products, how can you say that you have 100 per cent of your needs catered? You have zero per cent of the needs that are catered then.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: What about food and drinking water and things like that? It's correct that the UNHCR was providing that, whether or not it's 100 per cent in your view, but they were providing supplies to the civilian population; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, there wasn't. I don't think you know the area. It is an area where people live off their farm produce, their pigs they raise, their crops. The UNHCR did not provide them with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It's correct here what's referred to about obstructions to the passage of aid convoys to the Bihac enclave through RSK territory, you were aware of such obstructions at the time; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But I fail to see where the convoys would have come from if they were crossing. They could have come from Croatia, if they had to cross the RSK to go to the Bihac pocket. I can't understand which route they took, because all the supplies for the 5th Corps of Dudakovic was regularly daily supplied from Bosnia. They didn't lack anything. So I really fail to understand which route was taken or the meaning of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the second paragraph, and maybe that will help clarify it. There, it's written: "Since our last meeting only four convoys were allowed in the Bihac enclave, and the last convoy team has been prevented from returning to Zagreb since the 28th of February. Although fighting may be occurring in the area through which they plan to drive, there are other safe routes to leave Bihac such as the one through Petrovo Selo where no fighting is occurring at the moment." So it appears that these convoys were going between Croatian territory in the Bihac pocket, and to do so they had to cross RSK territory but they were being obstructed. Now, do you know anything about that? Did you know about that at the time? Can you offer any comment on it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I can give you a very simple comment. The letter is dated March 1995. As of the summer of 1994, until the beginning of 1995, there was fighting in the Bihac pocket between the 5th Bosnian Corps of Dudakovic and the men of Fikret Abdic. If it was impossible to go through to the Bihac pockets, it was because of the Muslim army not because of the Serbs. At any rate, the 5th Corps was always very well supplied. Those that did not get supplies, they were the people from -- the Serbs from Krajina, so this is absolutely nonsensical.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So your position is that this letter is not correct. It wasn't the RSK that was obstructing access to Bihac, it was just the fighting. That's what you're saying, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But of course, yes, that's what I'm saying. It's the access through Bosnia to the Bihac pocket, it was totally controlled by the 5th Corps. So if somebody was obstructing, it was the 5th Corps; they controlled the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So just so that it's clear to everyone. When you talk about the 5th Corps, you're talking about the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, correct, the Bosniak army?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Headed by General Atif Dudakovic who, as far as I'm aware, was not indicted for the crimes he committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And are you saying that the 5th Corps even controlled the boundary with RSK? That there was no way that you could get from the RSK into the Bihac pocket without going through the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: It is the 5th Corps that drove all the men of Fikret Abdic to Krajina at that time, so he was the one in control of the area. On the other hand, in -- when there was the Storm operation, when over 200.000 Serbs were expelled from Krajina, they could not receive any aid whilst they were in the Banja Luka area because the Muslims, Bosnians, were against the passage of humanitarian convoys. Whenever there was obstruction, it was done by the Bosnian Muslims not by the Serbs because the Serbs needed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just look at one last paragraph in this document and it's the third one. I don't -- well, maybe I don't need to read it out, but it says here that: "Because of the obstruction by the RSK, the UNHCR is forced to suspend humanitarian assistance to the UNPAs and Velika Kladusa until regular access to Bihac has been opened." So, at least from the point of view of the UNHCR, it was the RSK that was obstructing humanitarian assistance in this case, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, it's quite delirious, that's what this letter says, but it is absolutely nonsensical. I repeat it. This goes to show that those who believe in this letter did not know anything about the military situation prevailing in the Bihac pocket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, let me just sort of say we try to speak with respect here. It's the second time you're using that word "nonsensical." I'd ask you to stop using it, okay? And in any case, let me just say that whatever you may think about the nonsensical -- this man being nonsensical, the addressee of the letter would have understood what was being said to him and he should have been able to say if indeed it was nonsensical and it was impossible for the RSK to implement what was being requested of them. I don't know whether any response in that line did come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually could this document receive an exhibit number, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 1009.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, I'm going to ask you a couple questions, if you don't know -- if you don't have any information on these topics, you can tell me. After the cease-fire agreement in March of 1994 -- this is in the context, by the way -- you talked about conditions in the Krajina, including economic conditions, and so I have a couple of questions about -- following on from that topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Martic has a note for his counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me start my question again because I was being confusing. You spoke about conditions in the Krajina, including economic conditions, and I just had a couple questions following on from that. Isn't it true that after the March 1994 cease-fire agreement, the Serb side stalled and obstructed negotiations on an economic agreement up until December of 1994?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know. As far as I know this information is not correct. One thing is certain: The cease-fire agreement was not respected by the Croat side.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Nor by the Serb side, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR reports show that there were regular and irregular units of the Croatian army that penetrated into Herzegovina and Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, but my question was about the Serb side. The Serb side also violated the March 1994 cease-fire agreement; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: When did they do so and where?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly before August of 1994. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me take a little detour here and show you Exhibit -- document which is not yet in evidence. It's ZA024795 to 4799.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could see that on our screens, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you say 024 or 042?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me just read it again so that hopefully I get it right. ZA024795.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's fine, actually. This is the page I was looking for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you see in front of you another letter from the UNPROFOR force commander, and it's dated the 15th of August, 1994, and this one is addressed to General Celeketic. And in the first paragraph there, just quickly, it says: "I know your personal commitment towards the consolidation of the 29 March cease-fire agreement. In that respect, I want to express my deepest concerns as well as a strong protest for the continuous and increasing violations of the cease-fire agreement. I consider these violations a list of which is attached to this letter as extremely serious insofar as they are not any longer the result of regrettable local initiatives, but of a deliberate plan which simply ignores the commitment signed by your political authorities." Having seen this, do you accept that the RSK was violating the 29 March, 1994, cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But of course not. This is just small-talk. There is no fact, no date that is given, nothing accurate, and this is dated the 15th August, 1994, when the 5th Bosnian Corps was attacking Krajina through the Bihac pocket and was pushing, driving, all the Muslim from the Bihac pocket towards Krajina. So there is not a single fact in there. It's really --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, this --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: -- sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Lieutenant-General Bertrand de Lapresele - I say that very poorly - but this person was your commander when you were in UNPROFOR, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, he was, and he gave me a medal. He rewarded me, and this shows this dual standards all the time. You know, on the one hand you have the 5th Bosnian Corps who enters the Krajina, and all you can see in this letter by UNPROFOR is very vague accusations of violations of a cease-fire agreement. However, the Flash and Storm operations were true violations of this agreement. All this is just mere talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I don't want to spend too much time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But can we move to -- I guess it's pages 4, page 4 of the -- this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My document is -- ends at 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Oh really, Your Honour, I'm sorry. Because there is an attachment to this which details the cease-fire violations but it's -- I'll move on, Your Honour. I'll leave it at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Well, well let me just read it out to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, according to attachment to this document regarding Serbian violations of the cease-fire agreement, as of the 14th of August, 1994, it says: "In Sector East, there were nine violations regarding heavy weapons, the failure to withdraw heavy weapons, one violation regarding monitoring of the ZOS."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just wanted to say to you I'm with you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLAKC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My page 3 talks about what your page 4 talks about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Oh, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It continues: "In Section West, there were two violations of the cease-fire agreement by failure to monitor the ZOS. In Sector North, four violations regarding heavy weapon withdrawal and four violations regarding monitoring the ZOS. In Sector South, nine violations regarding monitoring the ZOS." Is it nevertheless your position, sir, that all of this is, as you say small-talk, it's not fact? It's all fabrication?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I maintain what I said because this sort of document has no value at all. Not even a single wounded is mentioned, nothing is said as to who fired, whether there was a response fire. Next to that you have the Flash operation, the Storm operation, with hundreds of casualties, hundreds of dead, with shells falling. That -- these are violations of the cease-fire agreement. This document here has no value whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. You realise that in August 1994 there had been no Flash operation, no Storm operation, right? So of course, you can't expect to see that in a document from August of 1994, can you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But this has been prepared. We know that there were infiltrations in the time before this in order to prepare for these operations. And those operations were real violations of the cease-fire. You don't even see a single wounded in this paper, so what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be admitted into evidence as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit Number 1010.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, perhaps you don't know about this, but maybe you do so I'll ask you: Isn't it the case that in 1994 and 1995, the RSK rejected any proposed agreement that did not include independence, including the so-called Z-4 plan?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: It is wrong. You refer to the Zagreb Z-4 plan. If there was no agreement, it is because President Tudjman said that he did not want to sit together with Milan Martic at the negotiating table. The Krajina Serbs were ready, were willing, to do any kind of compromise and concessions. It is the president, President Tudjman, who refused to sit down with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Let me read you one quote, and it's from an exhibit, 1003, which is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I don't want to bring it up on the screen, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But let me just read out to you a very short quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I just want to read out a very short quote from an RSK official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Black.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Is not this area on the list of prohibited subjects or not? Because if we don't allow the Defence to go into it, it seems rather unfair to permit to you cross-examine on it. Is it -- am I recollecting correctly that it is one of the topics?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I have a moment to confer with counsel?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do agree that the Z-4 plan was one of the things mentioned by the Trial Chamber - actually I have the cite there but not at hand - but this is in response to the witness's testimony about economic conditions, about the fact that the Serbs were always delighted to negotiate and that the Croatian side was the one who was violating the cease-fire agreements and not negotiating in good faith. I don't intend to spend have very much time on it, but I would ask to be able to put one more question to him on it, since it is something that was discussed in his testimony on direct examination and further in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Maybe we could hear the question first.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'll put the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, if you could just wait a second after I ask you the question, and then the Judges will decide whether or not you have to answer it. Would you agree with the following statement by a RSK official whom I won't name? "There was no willingness to talk about peace or making peace our dominant option. The prevailing policy said that the Ustashas were the opponent. This was to be no discussion with them except through the sight of the rifle. We would accept the international community's proposals about likely negotiations, but only to block them eventually with concrete moves."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That's my question, Your Honour. And, Your Honour, I believe this goes to what the witness has testified about, negotiations between the sides and the condition in Krajina in 1995. But I'm in your hands as to whether or not to proceed to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Black, the Trial Chamber will allow the question, but it is to be kept extremely limited, to ensure that there is no offence of the Trial Chamber's order, and subject to re-examination limited by the Defence in respect of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I'm extremely grateful for your guidance, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Mr. Barriot, now if you remember the question, please go ahead and answer, whether or not you agree with that statement that I read out to you.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Listen, you're asking me to give a response to a document that you do not present, mentioning somebody whose name you hide, so it's like fog in a tunnel. Still, I'm going to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Please go ahead and just continue.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: My answer is this: The only side that refused to negotiate was the Croat side, and as was shown later on. They were the one who is attacked Western Slavonia and Krajina. They were the ones who massacred the civilian population. If that is the willingness to negotiate, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I think I'll move on to the next topic, and that's the alleged involvement, according to you, of the United States in Operation Storm. I don't intend to spend a lot of time on this, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, objection. Is not Operation Storm also on the index of banned topics?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is. But I thought what he was saying was: "... and that's the alleged involvement, according to you, of the United States in Operation Storm. I don't intend to spend a lot of time on that." But unless -- are you going to talk about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. On 53 of the transcript, and I believe in other places, the witness talks about this and he makes allegations about things that happened. Page 53 -- that's just one example, but about the United States army planes attacking, about this Military Professional Resources Incorporated. This is stuff that the witness addresses on direct; we do not accept it. And there are things I think I need to put to him. It's only fair, Your Honour. The witness can't testify about something on direct and then we be then excluded from cross-examining on it. That's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: It was done incidentally, though. It was -- the evidence that was given was more incidentally, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: It happened on several occasions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Yes, I will admit that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Page 53, what lines are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Page 53, lines -- line 25.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And this is under direct?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm trying to see if I can find other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh: "Radar had spotted airplane."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Actually, I'm told 53 was cross. Let me find the cite, Your Honour, because this was discussed in direct. I believe it was the last topic discussed before my cross-examination, before the break. I apologise for not having a cite more quickly at hand, Your Honours, but I'm finding it right now. For instance, at page 25, there is, at line 6, a question about this relation between the American organisation and the Croatian authorities. According to our searches, this MPRI, Military Resources Incorporated, is mentioned five times in the transcript. Paragraph 24 it is said that: "MPRI, under the command of the Pentagon," there are a number of references there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These comments by the witness were not answers to my question. I did not put a single question in connection with Operation Storm or any possible involvement by American elements in that operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the witness testified about those things, and you didn't stop him, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So they are on record. Those statements are on record. What the witness has put on record I think that the Prosecution is entitled to cross-examine him on -- on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'll try to be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you know the topic that I'm referring to now. First of all, this idea of United States planes attacking Knin at the beginning of Operation Storm, I think you said. Isn't it the case that the incident you're talking about was where planes flying under the NATO flag attacked an RSK surface-to-air missile defence site near Knin which had locked on to NATO planes, locked on their firing mechanisms? I think you referred to this somewhere in your testimony. That's the same incident we're talking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, but you are changing things. This incident is very clear. The US planes, now you mentioned NATO. That's wrong, that's false. It's not NATO, or else you have to show us the NATO intervention order. You know for NATO to start air-strikes, the NATO ambassadors have to sign an order. So it's not NATO that intervened. It is the US, from the aircraft carrier Theodore Roosevelt, and then if they struck the anti-aircraft defence in Knin, not because they were a threat to them, they wanted to destroy it so that the Croatian army could destroy -- could bomb Knin for the MiG 23 to intervene peacefully in -- and that's the true.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters ask counsel to slow down when they put questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll try to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what about the witness himself? Mr. Witness, you must also please slow down when you speak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: We'll both try to go slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: You're aware, sir, that human Rights Watch was of the view and published a report that this was NATO planes and gave the description that I've just given, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, look, I stop you right there. I can see what document you are thinking of. What does Human Rights Watch rely on? On an article published in an American newspaper. Human Rights Watch did not see that themselves. They rely on an article published in the American press, and I'm familiar with it. So first of all, this is second-hand knowledge based on an article; secondly, Human Rights Watch is not at all in a position to say whether it was NATO or the United States that intervened. I do not think that they have the necessary military knowledge to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. But you do, and according to you it was all just -- it was just a hoax, it was a justification so the Americans could attack Knin. That's your evidence, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, of course. You've got American aeroplanes who would fly over Knin. Of course they are going to be spotted by the radar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So you have American airplanes that fly over Knin. Obviously, the radars will spot them and then they will bomb the radars. Saying that we have been spotted by these radars is just a lame excuse, to destroy the batteries and to allow the intervention of the Croats as part of the storm operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I want to move away from this topic. But with regard to Military Professional Resources Incorporated, this private company you talked about, first of all, this was a private company and not a branch of the United States government, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. I do not agree with you. Yeah, we can talk about MPRI, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, actually let me -- sir --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Do you want me to answer your questions or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Yes, I want you to answer my specific question. Okay? That's our role here. I put questions and you answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, let's -- excuse me, sir. Excuse me, sir. Look here. I'm talking to you. Now, here he asks questions, you answer. You don't postulate somethings next to the answer. Listen to me. I'm talking. I'm talking. Okay? You listen to the question carefully and you answer the question. Okay? You don't go into debate with -- fine. Listen to the question and answer the question. I'm going to be listening very carefully and I will tell you if you're not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: The question is narrowly, this MPRI is a private company and not a branch of the United States government; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The answer should be yes or no and stop there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It's under the orders of the Pentagon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: So according to you, this is a company that's either part of the United States government or taking orders from the Pentagon? Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, you've understood me perfectly. It's a way of -- for the American government to be able to intervene on the sly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I suppose your basis for there is, again, intelligence services? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. I could give you a very long answer about that if you want to have all the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: I don't think we need the details. Let me just put one thing to you for your comment and we can go on to the next. I'm glad you find your experience here a humorous one, sir, but if we could be serious for a few more minutes, I'll finish your cross-examination. Let me just put one more thing to you. Isn't it the case that MPRI provided training on human rights and leadership issues. They did not arm the Croats, and the United States respected the arms embargo regarding the former Yugoslavia? If you disagree with me, you can just say so, and we'll move on.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I disagree with you completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. You've always considered the charges in this Tribunal against Milan Martic to be illegitimate; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, and I stand by my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that position is one that you formed long before this trial started, right, without seeing any of the evidence that was led at this trial?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. That's not the case. I've been working for more than 12 years on the history of the Serbs in the Krajina region and I believe I know their history very well indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My question was that you formed this opinion before this trial started and before you were able to see the evidence that was led at this trial concretely, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, but I knew most of the evidence before the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Earlier we saw the open letter to your friend Milan Martic, which reminds me, Your Honour, I forgot to move that into evidence. I wonder if just that section, the article along with the two pages of English could be admitted into evidence and we'll make sure the proper pages are uploaded into e-court?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the open letter to friend be admitted -- it is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, together with the French version?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will become Exhibit number 1011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just a couple more quick questions while I have this book. In addition to the article we saw earlier, there is another article in here called, "What Justice for Krajina" in which you basically defend Milan Martic against the charges which he faces here today, correct? Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I've written so many articles and so many books about Krajina that I do not quite see what article you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: This one is called "Quelle justice pour la Krajina". It's Y0061918, if we need to see it on the screen. I hadn't intended to go into it in any detail. Is that an article that you recall?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Based on the title, yes, I suppose that I indeed submit all the arguments to show that Krajina was the victim of a great injustice.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And Mr. Martic, in particular, you also think has been the victim of a great injustice here, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course. That's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Just one other article worthy of -- that I think I should mention. There is also an article about Srebrenica here. Let's see if I can find the title of this one. It's "Quelques verites sur Srebrenica et sorsu qui recollect." I apologise if my pronunciation isn't that great, but in this article you basically suggest that the crimes in Srebrenica have been exaggerated and that the Bosnian authorities sacrificed Srebrenica to gain the sympathy of the international community, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I'm not the one who is saying it. It's General Morillon himself who said it and I don't think that you can challenge what General Morillon said because he was there in Srebrenica. He's presented as the defender of Srebrenica and he himself said that. Alija Izetbegovic decided to sacrifice Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And that's the argument you make in that article in that book, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Of course, I'm using the arguments of the people who were there and whose word you can't challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: And I take it that you stand by everything that you say in that book, you stand by that here today, it's still your view, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I do not see the link between that and between the trial of Mr. Milan Martic. Yes, but I stand by the position I expressed in this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. Not with standing judgements rendered by this Tribunal that have come to very different conclusions about what happened in Srebrenica, for instance, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honours. I believe that the witness observed, rightly, that the trial associated with Srebrenica has nothing whatsoever to do with this trial, so I fail to see the relevance of my learned colleague's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, I think his views and his clinging to views, despite the work of this Tribunal or other evidence, is relevant to his credibility. That's why I'm asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any reply, Mr. Perovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think that this is the right answer from the Prosecutor. I continue to maintain that this is an irrelevant question because Srebrenica has nothing whatsoever to do with the indictment against Milan Martic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you say something in response to the argument that he's testing credibility?

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I can say that it is in an inappropriate way that he seeks to discredit this witness by the story about Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll just put this question and then move on. I'll just put the same question and try to get an answer and then move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, you stand by these views about Srebrenica and other things in your book today, notwithstanding the judgements that have been rendered by this Tribunal which have come to different conclusions, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I stand by the statements of General Morillon, which he made before a commission at the French assembly. This is in the archives of the French parliament, and he stated very clearly that Izetbegovic sacrificed Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking about you, not General Morillon. I think it's a simple question, and once you answer it we can get on. But you stand by these positions notwithstanding the, sort of, contrary findings of the Tribunal, right?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, in the same way as I stand by the position of General Michael Rose, General Pierre Geloire [phoen] and all the other generals who told the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters have missed some of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, another book which you co-authored with Ms. Crepin is "The Murder of a People," referring to the Krajina Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: It's not "The Murder of a People." It's based on a sentence written by Viktor Hugo, A People is Being Murdered." It's not exactly what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: That was the translation I got into English, so we are talking about the same book. Milan Martic contributed a preface on that book, correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Can you please clarify that? What is the original title of the book in question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The title is "A People is Being Murdered," the Serbs from the Krajina region -- Krajina Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: When was this book published, and in which language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The book was published in French in September 1995, by L'age d'homme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. You may go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We can look at the book. I have not asked that any parts be translated into English, but the original is at 03593652 and continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, while that's being brought up, Milan Martic contributed a preface to this book, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milan Martic wrote the preface to this book because I asked him to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe there were also contributions by Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic, correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: If we could just look at one page, it's the page with the ERN 03593659, and this, sir, I think you'll recognise, is part of your own introduction or preface to the book. And if we could look at the top right-hand corner, please. Sir, so that it's on the transcript, could you please read out for us that paragraph that begins "C'est pour moi ..."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: "It is for me a huge honour to have in this books texts written by President Milan Martic, President Radovan Karadzic and General Ratko Mladic, united in the defence of the Serb people, and its Orthodox church, represented by Bishop Longin. They write in the honour of the memory of Prince Lazar and the Serb chevaliers who fell at the Battle of Kosovo Polje, on that terrible day of June 1389. They are the deserving heirs to these people and I would like to respectfully greet them."

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: My thanks to the French interpreters for that difficult translation and fast translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: But, sir, this is dated the 15th of August 1995. At the time, Milan Martic had been indicted for the shelling of Zagreb; the world was blaming Karadzic and especially Mladic for what happened in Srebrenica in July 1995. But you stood by those men, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. You're mischaracterising what I'm saying. I'm not sure you've read my book. This book, it was written at the time of the Storm Operation and the aim was to defend a people that had been the victim of the worst operation of ethnic cleansing that took place in the war in the former Yugoslavia. And if you read what Karadzic and Mladic wrote, there is nothing unacceptable in what they wrote. They just analysed the situation in the Bihac pocket. So you should not mischaracterise what I wrote and make suggestions that are totally inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Sir, I'm not characterising anything. We just read out your very own words. One last question: Do you still respectfully salute these three men today?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I believe that these men defended their people and that they performed this mission in a very difficult situation, in a situation of civil war. I'm not saying that atrocities were not committed on one side and on the other. But it was an atrocious civil war, and each one of them tried to defend their people, the people who they were responsible for.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: No further questions at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is this book now tendered?

utterances.speaker: MR. BLACK
utterances.text: Your Honour, since the part I was interested in was read out on the record, I hadn't intended to tender it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Perovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PEROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no redirect for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Perovic. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Well, I would like to ask you one very general question. You were asked about your opinion about this Court. Are you, Witness, regarding this Tribunal as a court against a people or individuals?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: To give you a candid answer, Your Honour, I believe, from the bottom of my heart, that this is a biased and partial Tribunal that was established to indict and to convict the entire Serb people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. I take your answer in the affirmative as to the question if this is a Tribunal against an entire people. How do you know? Did you reach this conclusion on your own; if not, who told you this?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I reached this conclusion after many years of work, many years of being present in the field. I believe that this Tribunal is another way of continuing the war waged against the Serbs, only with other means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: What do you mean, "in the field"? Is this Tribunal in the field?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, no. What I meant to say is that the Tribunal is continuing with legal means the work towards total -- until there is a total destruction of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Have you got any education in international law?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, but I work in close cooperation with Maitre Jacques Verges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: With whom?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Jacques Verges, who has all the legal arguments at his disposal that could be developed, also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Could you spell out the family name, for the record. And that's enough from me.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: His first name is Jacques. His family name is V-e-r-g-e-s. He's the most famous French lawyer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: This is always a value judgement, isn't it? But I pass now to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Barriot, the two buildings which were targeted as military targets, which you have given evidence you believed were the Ministry of Defence and the military airfield, were you given any reason why those specific buildings were targeted?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I did not receive any other information. I must say I didn't ask for it either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. And you spoke of the circumstances under which you came to leave the French army, and you mentioned the fact that there was a complaint by a Monsieur Granic that you had not complied with an obligation of reserve. What is that obligation of reserve? Could you explain what it is.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, Mate Granic, he's the former Minister of Foreign Affairs in Croatia. He complained with the French government, because I was together with Serb local population and starting from that, Charles Millon, who was the French Defence Minister, who ordered for me to be arrested for several days and to be punished because I did not maintain the reserve that is imposed on military, because, in other words, I had expressed my views. Without having the authorisation to do so from my hierarchy, I had expressed my opinion on a sensitive subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems to me that you feel very passionately about this subject matter of the Krajina and the circumstances of the Serbs in the Krajina over the relevant period. How many publications in all have you authored and published in relation to this subject of the victimisation, as you perceive it, of the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: To date, I have authored five books and over 100 articles, together with Eve Crepin, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Now, there is one area in which you seem to be a little bit at variance in your evidence. You spoke initially about the circumstances of the people in the Krajina and the difficulty they had in terms of having access to basic necessities, and I believe food was mentioned as one of them. But I believe at a later stage now, when asked about the Bihac pocket, you indicated that one should remember that this was farming people and they produce their food and had access to food, as a means of undermining what counsel had put to you in terms of the obstruction of the passage of humanitarian aid. So could you tell me which one is true? Or is it a case where, in some areas, there was the absence of these -- the basic necessity of access to food, but in other areas there was the farming and the people were able to sustain themselves? Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is no disparity, nor variance. Look at what I stated. I never said that there were people who did not have enough to eat. I did mention basic necessities as to medical supplies and hospitals, school books at school, on candles and soap, but I told you that altogether they did not need any food assistance because basically there were people from a rural area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much for that clarification. No further questions of you, Mr. Barriot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. It's now my turn to ask you a few questions, sir. Let me just start here. Is Ms. Eve Crepin also an anaesthetist?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Eve Crepin is a specialist nurse, specialised in emergency care and intensive care.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You testified this morning that because of the economic situation in the Krajina, Croats decided to leave the Krajina to other cities; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember, Mr. President. I said that some stayed whilst others left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, was it only the Croats who were so affected by this economic situation that they left?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, but they were the only ones who were able to go because the Serbs had to stay. Only the Croats could go somewhere else in Croatia. But the Serbs could not precisely because they had just been expelled from the rest of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, the Muslims, they sought refuge in Krajina, when they were driven out of Bosnia and out of the Bihac pocket. But they didn't go to Croatia. They came from an area where they were still more miserable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And they didn't find it necessary to -- when they get to the Krajina and find the bad economic situation, they didn't find it necessary to also then leave the Krajina, go to Croatia, they coming from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: As soon as they were able to leave, they did, especially those 40.000 Muslims from the Betanija and Turan camps. They arrived in August 1994 and they left again in January 1995. But it's true that the Krajina area was not a nice place to live.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you didn't refer to them as having left the Krajina. You only referred to the Croatians. Why didn't you mention them?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: You know that for a Muslim it was not a very good idea to go to Croatia. You know that there is not even a single mosque in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that. I just want to know why they didn't leave. And was Bosnia the only place -- Croatia the only place they could go to? They could have gone to some other places. They could have gone to Serbia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But, Mr. President, do you speak about the Muslims or the Croats?
