utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm talking about the Muslims.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, whenever the Muslims wanted to seek refuge in Krajina, they could find a place to be. Whenever they wanted to go again, they did. Nobody was against their coming or leaving in Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question to you was: Then why was it only the Croats that you mentioned as having left the Krajina because of the economic situation? Why didn't -- and now you have said that -- you're saying that the Muslims could also leave. Why didn't you mention them in your evidence-in-chief, these Muslims?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But I did speak about the Muslims at length, especially about those who came to be treated from the Bihac pocket in Glina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not listening to my question. I'm not saying you didn't speak about Muslims. I said you didn't mention them as people who also left the Krajina because of the economic situation. Please listen to my questions and answer them. Not your own.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, I do answer your question. They could go -- they could only go to Bosnia. Anyway, they could not go to Croatia. So whenever some left, they did go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand that you say they could go. My question to you is: Why didn't you mention them in your evidence-in-chief, when you were asked -- when you talked about the bad economic situation, why did you say only -- why did you say Croats decided to leave the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I stated, because the problem, the tension, that existed was between the Serbs and the Croats. There was no tension between the Serbs and the Muslims. This is the reason why I mentioned the Croats only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's more like an explanation. You indicated that you discussed with Mr. Martic on the subject of the shelling of Zagreb, and in your discussions it became clear that he had not ordered the shelling but he took the responsibility as president. Do you remember that testimony by you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes, I do, Mr. President. That's how I perceived it and that's the memory I have of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When did you have this discussion with Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Well, I had several discussions with him, towards the end of 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Towards the end of 1995. And towards the end of 1995, that was before you wrote the article that was shown to you, that is said to be dated the 15th -- I'm sorry -- the 15th of September 1997.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, in fact, the publication date is not a good one, because this article was published before that date, as I pointed out to the Prosecutor. It was published several times, and you have the late -- well, the latest publication date here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When was it first published?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I'm unable to answer you accurately. I wrote over 100 articles and I can't remember all the publication dates, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know whether the article -- your discussion with Mr. Martic was before or after writing the article? If you're not able to, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I think that this article was written before, precisely -- you know, this is -- when I say "under orders," I mean it's a way of putting it. A lot of insistence is put on these three words, because for me it was a desperate reaction by the Serbs as a whole. There was an article on the Krajina Serbs. This is not a legal process, trying to ascertain guilt or responsibility. This is a way of speaking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you talking about? I'm not sure what you're answering to now. What are you telling me? I asked you a simple question: Was it before or after writing the article that you had the discussion with Mr. Martic? What are you answering to?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: I answered your question. I said that I had this discussion after writing the article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, when you say you think the article was written before precisely, and then you say "a lot of insistence is put on these three words," I don't know which three towards you're talking about. What has that got to do with my question? My question --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: But this is a very specific issue of the responsibility one might have, because the Prosecutor insisted on order, upon orders given by President Martic, and I wanted to show that this is just a general expression, that it was not at all to demonstrate guilt. This is what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There was the matter -- when you write articles and when you write books, what is the purpose? I suppose the purpose is to document the truth, isn't it, as you see it? This is for posterity.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Of course, of course. But the truth was that the Serbs were being massacred in Western Slavonia and they had a very desperate reaction of self-defence. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me warn you once again. Please listen to my question and answer my question and my question only. I'm asking you, when you write -- the purpose for your writing is to tell the truth. You can say yes or you can say no. I don't need a long explanation, okay? When you write, like when you talk here - you've been telling us several times that you took the oath this morning to tell the truth - you write truthfully.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to be sure that you write truthfully, you investigate and check your sources before you write, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And but that notwithstanding you still go and write inaccuracies in your books. Why do you accuse Mr. Martic of having ordered the shelling when, in fact, he hasn't? You are now telling an untruth to those who read the book.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, no, not at all. I did not accuse President Martic of ordering the shelling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said in your article he ordered it. You only corrected the article this morning in court. You said he ordered the shelling of Zagreb because of the shelling of Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No, no, this is not what I said. I said that as a president, he took the responsibility for this act of self-defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That is the explanation you gave today in court. That is not what you wrote in the document. You explained that what you wrote in the document was incorrect because you have since established that, in fact, he didn't order it. So what is in that article is incorrect. You're telling the world an inaccuracy. Do you realise this? On your own version.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean, "No"? No, what? You don't realise it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No. I say no to the question you put to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is: Do you realise this? So if you don't realise it, I'll make you aware, because that article -- in that article you say Mr. Martic ordered the shelling.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK BARRIOT
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Anyway, it is long past the time for -- I'm sorry, I didn't realise the time. We will stop there. We'll carry on tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, sir, in the same court. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
